title: The Sum of All Fears
full_review:
Cunning neo-Nazi terrorists bring the U.S. and Russia to a nuclear showdown in the horrifying thriller "The Sum of All Fears" (Paramount).

���� This is the fourth instance of a Tom Clancy espionage novel turned into a movie, but this is a prequel, in which key character Jack Ryan is a young and inexperienced CIA analyst played by Ben Affleck. Previously, Alec Baldwin in "The Hunt for Red October" and Harrison Ford in "Patriot Games" and "Clear and Present Danger," portrayed the tough, fast-thinking spy.

���� Loosely adapted from the 1991 novel of the same name and set in the present, lowly Russian expert Ryan is suddenly called to advise CIA director William Cabot (Morgan Freeman) about new Russian president Nemerov (Ciaran Hinds looking like a handsome Bela Lugosi), whom Ryan has studied and considers a moderate. Cabinet members and national security advisers around U.S. President Fowler (a short-tempered James Cromwell) think otherwise, however, suspecting Nemerov is an extremely dangerous and
hawkish hardliner.

���� Meanwhile, a shadowy group of international neo-Nazis (led by Alan Bates) has acquired an unexploded atom bomb newly uncovered in the desert sands after a 1973 Israeli fighter jet crash. Once put back in working order by three rogue Soviet scientists who foolishly think they will be paid a fortune, the bomb is to be transported and exploded at the upcoming Super Bowl game in Baltimore -- with the President Fowler in attendance. The terrorists expect Russia to be blamed and suffer nuclear retaliation, leaving a power vacuum they are prepared to fill.

���� A year ago the film might have described as a sleekly made thriller, which it is, but the devastation of Sept. 11 has given it an extra layer of horror. Although Ryan is still the resourceful hero, the unthinkable does happen midway through the film, leaving him scrambling to prevent a worldwide catastrophe. A story that once might have seemed far-fetched can now ratchet up fear and dread in already nervous public. It's certainly not a movie for those still emotionally fragile from having lost anyone in the terrorist attack, and it still may be too soon for many others. In fact, given the disastrous turn of events the movie takes, one can find fault with presenting a film in which thousands are killed as an exciting thriller.

���� Director Phil Alden Robinson, however, keeps the trio of story lines about the strategies of the terrorists, the Americans and the Russians moving along at a good clip as Ryan races against the clock to pinpoint the true perpetrators of the attack. Affleck captures his character's insecure new-kid-on-the-block status fairly well under the older and wryly wiser Freeman. Ryan's love affair with a resident surgeon (Bridget Moynahan) is weakly swirled into the plot to give a minimum female presence and to provide an upbeat ending, but precisely that romanticized ending tends to trivialize the movie's tragedy in disturbing ways.

���� There's also Liev Schreiber's superspycharacter and other secret operatives whose murderous actions at the end are meant to reassure the audience but which raise moral questions that are never addressed.

���� Despite the handsome lensing and suspenseful scenes, it's hard to merely enjoy and accept this film as just escapist entertainment.

���� Because of some catastrophic and recurring violence, the issue of vigilante justice, an implied affair, intermittent profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV, -- adults with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
